list.listitem: Keep a high index of suspicion for lightning strike in any patient found unconscious in the open, especially following storm events. C
If loss of consciousness, treat with BLS or ACLS protocol. C
If cardiac or respiratory arrest has not occured within one hour following injury, death is unlikely. Permanent sequelae of varying degrees are found in roughly three quarters of victims. C
Lichtenberg figures are indicative of lightning strike, but are not always present. C
Lightning strike injuries include a range of injury, including death.
Keraunopathology is the study of lightning-induced pathology or damage.
Lightning is the second leading cause of weather-related death in the United States (second only to flooding).

Injuries are variable by location, season, time, and gender. Injuries are most common in mountainous regions. 90% of injuries occur in spring and summer months. 70% occur in the afternoon or evening time. 85% of lightning-related injuries are in men.
Approximately 400 injuries and 40 deaths annually are associated with lightning strikes in the United States.
8 million lighning strikes occur daily, or approximately 50 times per second worldwide.

Types of lightning strikes :
Side splash/flash: the person is struck by lightning indirectly by being near an objuct that was struck (following the path of least resistance). This is the most common cause.
Direct strike: the person is directly struck by lightning (uninterrupted).
Contact strike: the person was in contact with an object that was struck by lightning.
Ground current/step voltage/stride voltage: lightning strikes the ground and travels to the person via ground conduction.
Blast injury: blunt trauma occurs due to the lightning shockwave.

Basics of Injury:
Classic injury: associated with side splash/flash, direct strike, or ground current. The body becomes part of the electrical circuit, causing entrance and exit wounds. Exposure is absorbed internally and may cause cardiac, pulmonar, and nervous system injury, until ultimately dissipating in the skin.
Mechanical injury: associated with contact strike or blast injury. The shock wave created by the lightning bolt is transmitted through the body. This may generate a shock wave of up to 20 atmospheres, and may cause barotrauma and physical trauma.
Flash or arc burn: when lightning current strikes and burns the skin, but does not enter the body.
Flame injury: secondary to clothes catching fire.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: The beginning and end of a storm are the most dangerous.
Lightning and thunder occurring less than 30 seconds apart means it is within about 5 miles, and increases the danger of lightning strike. The lightning’s tip can strike within 30 to 50 meters.
Season of highest risk: Summer months.
Locations of highest risk: Mountainous environments, especially southern and southeastern Unite States, such as Texas and Florida.

list.listitem: The safest place during a lighning storm is inside a building. Find a large enclosed space if possible, and avoid touching water or metal. If not, assume the "lightning position" which involves sitting or crouching with knees and feet close together. Creating one point of contact with the ground reduces the risk of injury if struck. C
If in a car, windows should be rolled up and persons should not touch any metal parts. C
Avoid being in an open space, near a tall structure, metal structure, or water. C

In a mountainous environment, persons should be off peaks and ridges by early afternoon. If unable to do so, climbers should tie off individually to avoid being connected to another person via one rope. C
Avoid water environments at all costs. If in a boat on open water, immediately return to the shore and get as far from the shoreline as possible. C
It is not recommended to leave a place of safety to rescue and resuscitate victims during a lightning storm. C
Consider a lightning strike in any unconscious person found outdoors following a storm event. The most common history is reported bystanders who witnessed the strike. C
Lichtenberg figures, a purple to dark-red feathering or ferning pattern on the skin, are indicative of lightning strike, but are not always present. C

A reported history of lightning strike or recent thunderstorm is most helpful to distinguish from other conditions. Dermatologic findings may be helpful, but other examination findings are typically non-specific. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Difficult to distinguish. Typically no dermatologic findings.
Difficult to distinguish. Often has vital sign abnormalities or altered mentation. Usually no dermatologic findings present.
History and bystanders significant. Dermatologic and neurologic findings of lightning strike hard to replicate.
Difficult to distinguish. Typically no dermatologic findings.

Difficult to distinguish. Typically no dermatologic findings.
Blood pressure typically not be elevated after lightning strike.
Difficult to distinguish based on mental status alone. Would likely have other clinical features suggesting etiology of encephalopathy.
Difficult to distinguish. May have other injuries or dermatologic findings more consistent with assault.
Difficult to distinguish. Electrical injuries may have significant burns, including entry wounds. History and location of injuries are key.

list.listitem: Patients may or may not remember the strike. Bystanders can help confirm the situation and specific details, such as if patient was around water, metal, etc.
Remove all clothing for a full physical examination.
Vitals: check temperature as hypothermia may be present. Blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate may be variable.
CNS: perform a full neurologic examination, ask orientation questions, evaluate motor strength of extremities, reflexes, and sensation.

Keraunoparalysis may occur involving some or all of the following findings in an extremity: paralysis, pulselessness, pallor, coolness, paresthesias. The physiologic mechanism is secondary to vasospasm from increased catecholamine release secondary to autonomic dysfunction. Patients will recover completely in the span of a few hours. A high clinical suspicion for this injury can help avoid unnecessary and risky interventions.

HEENT: check for signs of skull fracture or blunt injury to the head. Perform a detailed ear, nose, and throat examination, including evaluation of tympanic membranes, ossicular chain, and a detailed eye examination.
Cardiac: evaluate for arrhythmia, check pulses and capillary refill.
Respiratory: evaluate for respiratory compromise.
Abdominal: evaluate for signs of liver, renal, spleen or other internal injury.
Musculoskeletal: evaluate for blunt trauma injuries, compartment syndrome, fractures, or rhabdomyolysis.

Skin: perform a detailed skin examination of the entire body. Many types of burns can occur, but are most often superficial. They can include linear charring (“scald burns”, where sweat forms on body), thermal burns (where the skin was in contact with metal), and kissing burns (on flexor surfaces where skin was touching).Lichtenberg figures, a purple/dark-red feathering or ferning pattern on the skin, are pathognomonic of lightning strike, but not always present (see photos in Figure 1 ).
ECG may demonstrate ST-segment changes, T-wave changes, QT interval prolongation, atrial dysrhythmias, and AV or bundle branch blocks.
Cardiac markers are commonly elevated, but myocardial infarction is an uncommon injury.

Keraunoparalysis, a transient paralysis from the lightning strike, may mimic spinal cord injury. An extremity may be transiently cold, cyanotic, pulseless, and mottled. This usually resolves after several hours without intervention.
Consider laboratory studies including complete blood counts, electrolyte panel, creatine phosphokinase, urine myoglobin, and others based on history and examination.
Radiographic studies may include bedside ultrasound (FAST exam, RUSH exam), radiographs of extremities to assess for fractures, and CT scans to assess for intracranial and intra-abdominal injuries.
If unconscious, begin BLS or ALS algorithm as appropriate. See for suggested approach.
Begin BLS or ACLS immediately in a person struck by lightning with cardiopulmonary arrest. C
In the setting of a mass casualty incident, utilize reverse-triage principles, first targeting people with cardiac and respiratory arrest. C
Long-term neurorehabilitation is recommended for permanent neurologic injuries. C
Psychological support should be offered to patients struck by lightning. C
Long-term neurorehabilitation is recommended for permanent neurologic injuries.
Behavioral problems are common after a lightning strike and can have a delayed onset. If present, mental health care is recommended.
A support group is available: Lightning Strike and Electric Shock Survivors International, Inc. http://www.lightning-strike.org; e-mail: info@lightning-strike.org; phone: (910)346-4708.
Treat burns with routine burn care.
Refer to a burn center if more than 10% of the total body skin area is affected.
Admit for history of direct strike, loss of consciousness, keraunoparalysis, continued neurologic abnormalities, or abnormal cardiac testing (ECG, echocardiogram).
Maintain on telemetry for at least 24 hours following direct strike or abnormal cardiac testing.
Acute renal failure is a known complication. If abnormal examination or laboratory studies, consider hospitalization.
A wide range of ophthalmic complications can occur. If direct lightning strike or vision loss, refer to an ophthalmologist.
Transient hearing loss and tympanic membrane rupture are common. Follow-up evaluation with otolaryngologist for those with hearing loss is recommended.
Labile blood pressures and autonomic instability are possible after lightning strikes and may persist for weeks to months.
Neurologic sequela can be transient, intermediate, or prolonged.

Most patients who experience a lightning strike and do not experience cardiac or respiratory arrest survive, but permanent sequelae of varying degrees are found in roughly three quarters of victims. C
Approximately 30% of lightning strike victims will die within the first hour secondary to cardiopulmonary arrest.
Cranial burns have increased mortality. C
Recurring or continuing cardiac, neurologic, and psychological conditions can occur.
Follow-up with specialists should be considered for long-term management and sequelae. Specialists to especially consider are neurology, cardiology, opthalmology, audiology, and psychology.
Lightning strikes in pregnancy are rarely reported. There are no reported cases of maternal mortality, but literature suggests fetal mortality approaching 50%.
Other complications include placental abruption, uterine rupture, and premature labor onset. If the patient is greater than 20 weeks gestation, fetal monitoring is recommended.
